blogs.title: The Nexus of Violence: Why Cartels Targeting Political Activists Can Spoil Asylum Claims in Colombia
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Tenth Circuit's strict application of the 'political opinion' nexus standard in *Jimenez v. Bondi*. The court ruled that threats filed by a narco-trafficking leader aligned with the president through a property dispute, not because of the petitioners' support for the Liberal Party. We explore how the 'central reason' test creates a dangerous hurdle for asylum seekers where state-aligned violence is tied to local trade disputes, distinguishing between protected political grounds and offline turf wars.

blogs.title: Threats Are Not Persecution: The High Bar for Psychological Harm in Immigration Law
blogs.description: Examining the threshold for 'past persecution,' this article breaks down the Tenth Circuit's reliance on *Wiransane* and *Brandy* to dismiss claims based solely on threats and psychological distress. The opinion emphasizes that while physical injury isn't required, emotional distress or psychological impacts alone rarely suffice. We discuss the trend toward stricter definitions of 'harm' in the post-Sanchez era and how this opinion reinforces the need for evidence of tangible suffering beyond 'fear of persecution'.

blogs.title: The Burden of Proof on State Protection: Why 'Police Apathy' isn't Enough for a Government Unable/Unwilling Argument
blogs.description: Focusing on the 'Unable-or-Unwilling' prong of the asylum claim, *Jimenez* clarifies the evidentiary burden on petitioners to show systemic government failure versus isolated officer conduct. The court held that a single encounter with an indifferent officer or the lack of evidence regarding the population does not demonstrate that the Colombian government is unable or unwilling to protect citizens. We discuss the practical implications for the 'reporting requirements' and the necessity of proving systemic inaction rather than individual apathy.
